X – ENDER Space s.r.o. develops distributed ledgers for space applications. We want to enable satellite to satellite p2p trustless data exchange and decentralized control applications over Distributed Satellite System (DSS) missions and constellations. 

Our innovative project introduces a groundbreaking approach to satellite operations, leveraging the power of distributed ledger technology (DLT) to create a secure, efficient, and collaborative space environment. This technology, akin to blockchain, offers a decentralized platform where satellites can share and exchange data in a trusted manner, akin to a digital community in the sky.
Key Benefits:
- Cost Efficiency: By participating in this network, satellites gain access to a vast pool of data from others, significantly reducing the need for individual data collection missions. This shared approach leads to substantial cost savings in terms of time, resources, and operational expenses.

- Revenue Generation: Unique data collected by satellites becomes a valuable commodity. This system enables satellites to monetize their data by providing access to it for a fee, creating a new revenue stream and turning data collection capabilities into profitable assets.

- Data Integrity and Security: The DLT ensures that once data is recorded, it is immutable and tamper-proof. This guarantees the authenticity and reliability of the data shared within the network, fostering trust among all participants.

- Automated Transactions: The use of smart contracts automates data requests and transactions. This not only simplifies operations but also ensures fairness and transparency in data exchange, further enhancing the system's efficiency.

- Collaborative Space Environment: Our project promotes a cooperative approach to space operations, where satellites work together, sharing resources and information. This collaboration paves the way for more advanced and comprehensive space missions, benefiting all stakeholders involved.

In summary, our distributed ledger technology for space operations is not just a technological innovation; it's a strategic business move. It offers a dual advantage of cost savings and revenue generation while ensuring data security and fostering a collaborative space environment. This positions our technology as a game-changer in the space industry, offering immense value to satellite operators and stakeholders in the burgeoning space economy.

Tartu Observatory is an institute of University of Tartu. Tartu Observatory was established as an independent research institute in 1947 and merged to University of Tartu
since 1st January 2018. Tartu Observatory is the leading center of space research and technology in Estonia.
The research areas of Tartu Observatory are space technology, earth observation (EO), cosmology, and stellar physics.

Tartu Observatory has modern, well equipped facilities for research work, an excellent visitor centre and new laboratory complex. In 2012, a new laboratory complex at the premises of Tartu Observatory has been established for development and testing of new technologies including stations for development, prototyping, and assembly; facilities for climatic, thermal-vacuum, vibration, and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) testing; workshops for mechanical construction and repair works. The laboratories have independent and automatic control for temperature and humidity. Special conditions as electrostatic discharge protected environment (ESD), anechoic chamber, and cleanrooms equivalent to EN ISO 14644 Class 8 conditions have been established. Three rooms in cleanroom environment with total area of 100 m2 are available for optical measurements, where permanent setups for radiometric, photometric, spectral, and angular sensitivity calibrations are installed. Optical laboratory includes passive damping setup tables, one of them on separately built foundation for vibration-free measurements.
The laboratories of TO are accredited to ISO 17025:2017 and offer calibration and testing services to research institutions and industrial customers (https://kosmos.ut.ee/en/laboratory).

Satraka Ltd develops and markets an innovative and market-disruptive user terminal tracking antenna technology for LEO and MEO satellites, to provide broadband internet services.

The technology, trademarked as Satraka, in being patented internationally.

Satraka uses dual feed system and a shaped toroidal reflector surface to produce tracking and handover beams in one antenna. The tracking beam is created by the movement of the feed system which is a few kg mass, rather than the entire antenna which is hundreds kg mass. This reduces the complexity of the tracking system and the cost.

Satraka offers competitive advantages over all existing tracking antenna on the market or under development, in both technical performance and cost.

Satraka technology applies to terrestrial 5G/6G market too, providing multiple and identical high gain beams simultaneously.

Our clients, numbering over 1200 across the group as a whole, are mainly small and medium sized enterprises from a wide range of industries. entityDescription:
The Brandenburg Wilderness Foundation took the opportunity to found wilderness on the sites of four selected former military training grounds. Founded by private and public partners in 2000, it now owns and takes care of over 14,400 hectares that are unique in Germany for their size, lack of roads and wilderness development. The wilderness areas are located on the former military training grounds of Jüterbog, Heidehof and Lieberose south of Berlin and Tangersdorf north of Berlin. All of the purchased areas are designated nature reserves, some of them being additionally assigned FFH or SPA status. With the aim of supporting, experiencing as well as exploring wilderness (“Wildnis stiften, erleben und erforschen”) the Foundation has taken a holistic approach from the beginning, striving to promote wider knowledge of wilderness and to make its beauty and fascination accessible for the public.
We regularly record selected animal and plant species in wilderness areas. Our rangers study wolves and wildcats using photo traps and genetic samples, record nightjars and bats or observe warmth-loving newcomers such as the praying mantis. Forest development and the condition of various biotopes are also scrutinised. Scientific photo monitoring documents the natural succession. Every few years we commission a biotope type mapping, which is carried out using aerial photographs. This is also about recording succession. 

Making nature in its beauty and fascination accessible is the stated goal of Brandenburg Wilderness Foundation. The Foundation constructs hiking trails, picnic areas and vistas in selected areas. Visitors can discover the landscape on their own on the paths cleared of munitions. Furthermore guided hikes and bike tours offer exciting insights into areas that are normally not accessible.

FOTEC Forschungs- und Technologietransfer GmbH is the research subsidiary of the University of Applied Sciences Wiener Neustadt, Austria. Founded in 1998, FOTEC initiates and manages research, development, technology, and innovation projects. With more than 40 employees, it supports the University in implementing its research and development strategy for both bachelor’s and master’s programs.

With 20 people, the department of Aerospace Engineering has long experience, not only in terms of development of space electric and chemical propulsion systems for space applications, but also in terms of diagnostic systems and test stands to characterize their performances such as thrust balances, Retarding Potential Analyzers (RPAs) and Digital Faraday Cups (DFCs). Through the development of integrated electric propulsion systems such as the IFM NANO Thruster, FOTEC has built up knowledge in the field of measurement, control, high voltage, power electronics and firmware development. The focus is laid not only on high efficiency and performance but also on high reliability and radiation safety.
Recently FOTEC has reached an important milestone in the development of chemical mono- and bi-propellant thrusters based on green propellants to replace the carcinogenic propellant Hydrazine which is still in common use. In particular, the developed and tested catalysts for the mono-propellant thruster show outstanding performance in terms of reliability, stability, and longevity. FOTEC has also been developing Active Spacecraft Potential Control devices (ASPOC) for decades. NASA integrated 32 ASPOC devices on their two MMS satellite in 2015 to enable highly accurate magnetic field measurements. The ASPOC devices have been in operation since then and are still fully operational. These devices are currently being miniaturized for future application on smaller satellites (e.g., CubeSats).
A large aerospace engineering laboratory is available at FOTEC, equipped with modern high vacuum chambers of various sizes, as well as facilities for environmental tests (TVAC, shock, vibration, ATOX - currently in development) and devices for material investigation (SEM/EDX, various microscopes). A dedicated cleanroom for assembly as well as a cleanroom tent allow handling of sensitive space hardware and loading of the test facilities.

The Engineering Technologies department is an interdisciplinary team of 9 people with competences in additive manufacturing, chemistry, and mechatronics systems. Since 2014 several ESA-funded projects have been carried out with European partners and primes such as Thales Alenia Space or Airbus Defense & Space. The main objectives of the R&D work of the Engineering Technologies department is the transformation of existing manufacturing routes of mechanical components or assemblies into additive manufacturing. Some examples are the antenna deployment and pointing mechanism (ADPM) bracket from the NEOsat platform, various RF antenna components in the C- and Ku-band range, and flexible metal bellows. Furthermore, this department is involved in the ISRU topic (In-Situ Resource Utilization) and is working with Martian regolith simulants in representative Martian environmental conditions (reduced pressure and CO2 atmosphere). The laboratory is equipped with state-of-the-art additive manufacturing hardware, 3D-scanners, powder analyzing analyzers, and a machine shop for post processing and interface machining.

Company description: UNEP/GRID-Warsaw Centre was established on 17 September 1991 pursuant to the official agreement signed between the Director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Polish Government (Ministry of the Environment, Forestry, and Natural Resources), as a centre working within the Global Resource Information Database (GRID) network. Formally, the Centre has been established in the structures of the National Foundation for Environmental Protection (hence, it has the non-profit status).
The Centre actively co-operates with self-government authorities, educational institutions and private companies pursuing corporate social responsibility (CSR) principles in a wide range of projects devoted to effective environmental management, application of remote sensing, geographic information systems (GIS), and environmental education.
Specific areas of expertise and activity of the UNEP/GRID-Warsaw Centre entail the following:
· geoinformation and remote sensing: analyses of spatial data on environmental and socio-economic phenomena and processes; geodatabase development and maintenance (incl. data harmonisation according to the INSPIRE implementing rules); development and market application of GIS solutions and geoportals; practical implementation of result of scientific discovery related to novel geoinformation tools and methods;
· environmental governance and reporting: thematic mapping and geovisualisation, incl. 3D modelling; development of GIS and ICT applications to support decision making and spatial planning by public administration units; use of mobile GIS-based tools and techniques to support monitoring and rapid mapping activities; implementation of the INSPIRE Directive in Poland;
· capacity building: specialized trainings, workshops, seminars, conferences; e-Learning courses; educational materials and publications – targeted primarily at public administration bodies and related to the use of remote sensing tools, GIS tools and applications (with focus on open source solutions), spatial data for environmental management, spatial planning, crisis management, etc.
· environmental campaigns, environmental education, public participation: using modern multimedia and other ICT solutions; youth education and awareness building on issues related to environment/nature protection, community involvement, building ICT literacy; fostering public and inter-institutional consultations, e.g. in spatial planning procedures, aided by geoinformation tools and methods (geo-consultations); citizen science; CSR and sustainable business practices;
